title: fix: prevent double encoding and missing Content-Type in webhook replies
body:
## Summary

When webhook replies are enabled, grammY serializes the Bot API payload into a JSON string and passes it to `handler.respond(json: string)`. However, several framework adapters improperly handled this JSON string:

1. **Hono**: Used `c.json(json)`, which calls `JSON.stringify()` on the string argument, resulting in double-encoded JSON string literals (e.g. `"{\"method\":...}"`) instead of a JSON object. Fixed by setting the `Content-Type: application/json` header and returning `c.body(json)`.
2. **Next.js**: Used `response.status(200).json(json)`, which also calls `JSON.stringify()` and produces a double-encoded string literal. Fixed by setting `Content-Type: application/json` and using `response.send(json)`.
3. **Azure Functions v4**: Returned `{ jsonBody: json }`, which causes the `@azure/functions` runtime to execute `JSON.stringify(init.jsonBody)`. Fixed by returning `{ status: 200, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: json }`.
4. **NHttp**: Called `rev.response.status(200).send(json)` without setting the Content-Type header, defaulting to `text/plain`. Fixed by setting the `Content-Type: application/json` header.
5. **Worktop**: Called `res.send(200, json)` without headers, defaulting to `text/plain`. Fixed by passing `{ 'content-type': 'application/json' }`.

## Verification
- Added regression tests in `test/convenience/webhook.test.ts` verifying serialization and headers for `std/http`, `Hono`, `Next.js`, `azure`, `azure-v4`, `nhttp`, and `worktop`.
- All checks (`deno task dev` consisting of `deno fmt`, `deno lint`, `deno task test`, and `deno task check`) pass cleanly.
- `npm run backport` successfully emits Node.js / types without errors.

title: fix: reject HTTP error responses in InputFile downloads
body:
> [!NOTE]
> The fix was written by Claude Fable 5.1 high and Claude Opus 5.5 High on Claude Code CLI, and GPT-6 Astra xhigh in Codex CLI.
> The PR body and fix verification were done by GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh on Codex CLI and GPT-6 Astra xhigh in Codex CLI.

## Summary

Reject unsuccessful responses in `InputFile` downloads using `!response.ok`, before their bodies can be uploaded as file contents. Only HTTP 200–299 responses pass this check. Upload supported supplied response streams directly, avoiding a second fetch of `response.url`. On Node, this optimization targets responses returned by `node-fetch`, Node's native `fetch`, and imported Undici `fetch`; web recognizes native `Response` objects, matching Deno.

Fixes #971.

This change:

- checks `response.ok` in the Deno, Node, and web URL helpers and their direct response-body input paths
- aborts unsuccessful URL downloads immediately
- uploads supplied response bodies directly on Node when they expose a callable `Symbol.asyncIterator`; the declared `ResponseLike.body` type is `AsyncIterable<Uint8Array> | null`
- uploads native `Response` bodies directly on web using `instanceof Response`, matching Deno
- preserves the existing URL-fetch fallback on Node when a supplied response body is null or does not expose a callable async-iterator method
- throws `No response body!` for successful native `Response` inputs with null bodies on web, matching Deno
- rejects unsuccessful responses on the direct body path without consuming or cancelling their bodies; callers remain responsible for consuming or cancelling those bodies
- marks directly used response-backed inputs as consumed on all three runtimes, so reusing the same `InputFile` throws
- throws a plain source `Error` containing the HTTP status through the existing lazy upload error path
- adds regression coverage for rejected 300/404/599 URL responses, upstream signal abortion, accepted 299 streams, and rejected 404 `Response` inputs

## Why

`fetch()` resolves normally for HTTP error responses. Previously, a URL returning 404 or 503 could therefore produce a successfully delivered document containing the HTML error page, or a misleading Telegram media error such as `IMAGE_PROCESS_FAILED`.

Checking `response.ok` consistently requires a successful HTTP response across all three fetch implementations. URL downloads retain the existing redirect behavior and check the final response's `ok` value. A redirect ending at an HTTP 200 login page still passes this check.

Aborting a URL fetch started by grammY releases the connection without draining a potentially huge or endless unsuccessful response body. For a supplied response handled by the direct body path, grammY rejects the unsuccessful status and leaves the body untouched. The caller decides whether to consume or cancel that body.

Node recognizes the response structurally and checks that its body exposes a callable `Symbol.asyncIterator`. This accepts responses from `node-fetch`, Node's native `fetch`, and an imported Undici `fetch` without relying on their different `Response` constructors or concrete stream classes. [Node's built-in `fetch()` uses Undici](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.4.0/docs/api/globals.html#fetch). `node-fetch` supplies a Node `Readable` yielding `Buffer` chunks; native Fetch and imported Undici supply a WHATWG `ReadableStream` yielding `Uint8Array` chunks. All three support async iteration. Because `Buffer` extends `Uint8Array`, all three streams can be returned unchanged. The check does not depend on a global `ReadableStream` constructor.

Web uses `instanceof Response` to recognize native responses, matching Deno. It checks `response.ok` first, then throws `No response body!` if a successful response has a null body. Neither case falls back to fetching `response.url`. Other web objects with a `url` property still follow the existing `URLLike` fetch path.

Previously, Node and web treated supplied responses as `URLLike` inputs and fetched `response.url` again. The direct body path uses the already-fetched bytes and avoids that extra request. Null or non-async-iterable response bodies retain the URL-fetch fallback on Node. Successful URL streaming and the URL helpers' existing missing-body behavior remain unchanged.

## Node response bodies and support

The supported Node optimization is for responses returned by `fetch()`, not user-constructed `Response` objects. The table describes the final behavior of this PR; before this PR, Node treated supplied responses as `URLLike` inputs and fetched their URL again. The `node-fetch` rows refer to v2.7, the dependency used by grammY.

| Response origin / construction | `response.body` | Stream chunk type | Support / behavior with this PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `await nodeFetch(url)` | Node `Readable` | `Buffer`, which extends `Uint8Array` | Supported: return the existing stream directly; no second fetch. |
| `await globalThis.fetch(url)` | WHATWG `ReadableStream`, when non-null | `Uint8Array` | Supported: return the existing stream directly; no second fetch. |
| `await undici.fetch(url)` | WHATWG `ReadableStream`, when non-null | `Uint8Array` | Supported: return the existing stream directly; no second fetch. |
| Native or Undici `fetch()` with a null body, e.g. a HEAD or 204 response | `null` | None | Preserve URL fallback; do not throw merely because the supplied body is null. |
| `new nodeFetch.Response(string / Buffer / Uint8Array / ArrayBuffer)` | `Buffer` | None: the body itself is a buffer | User-constructed responses are unsupported; this body does not pass the async-iterator check, so use URL fallback. |
| `new nodeFetch.Response(blob)` | `Blob` | None: the body itself is a blob | User-constructed responses are unsupported; use URL fallback. |
| `new nodeFetch.Response(nodeReadable)` | The supplied Node `Readable` | Whatever that stream emits; not necessarily bytes | Unsupported construction, but it passes the async-iterator check and is returned directly; non-byte chunks can break the upload. |
| `new NativeResponse(...)` or `new UndiciResponse(...)` with ordinary string, byte-array, buffer, or Blob input | WHATWG `ReadableStream` | `Uint8Array` | Unsupported construction, but the stream passes the check and ordinary byte uploads may work. |
| `new NativeResponse(customReadableStream)` or `new UndiciResponse(customReadableStream)` | The supplied WHATWG `ReadableStream` | Whatever that stream emits; not necessarily bytes | Unsupported construction, but it passes the async-iterator check and is returned directly; non-byte chunks can break the upload. |
| `new Response(null)` from any of these implementations | `null` | None | User-constructed responses are unsupported; use URL fallback. |
| Custom response-like object with a standalone async iterable body | Arbitrary async iterable | Whatever the iterable yields | Passes the async-iterator check and is returned directly. Byte iterables can work, but this is outside the intended Fetch-source contract and chunk types are not validated. |

Every direct-body path checks `response.ok` before returning the stream. An unsuccessful status throws without consuming or cancelling the supplied body. If the supplied body does not pass the async-iterator check, the existing URL helper instead fetches `response.url` and checks that new response's status.

The check recognizes a callable async-iterator method, not the body's provenance or future chunk types. The byte-chunk expectation comes from the supported Fetch implementations. User-constructed responses can therefore pass the checks yet yield non-`Uint8Array` chunks. This is technically a breaking case compared with the former URL-only handling, but it is outside the intended use case. Constructed responses also commonly have an empty URL, so falling back does not guarantee a successful download.

Plain `Buffer` and `Uint8Array` bodies do not expose an async-iterator method, so they use the URL fallback. Ordinary `node-fetch` downloads expose async-iterable streams of buffers, not a buffer as the body itself. The stream representations and constructor behavior are visible in the [node-fetch download path](https://github.com/node-fetch/node-fetch/blob/v2.7.0/src/index.js#L243), [node-fetch body implementation](https://github.com/node-fetch/node-fetch/blob/v2.7.0/src/body.js#L31-L74), and [Undici body implementation](https://github.com/nodejs/undici/blob/v6.27.0/lib/web/fetch/body.js).

## Verification

The regression tests in `test/types.test.ts` cover the updated success criterion:

- URL responses with statuses 300, 404, and 599 reject with an error containing the HTTP status, and the signal passed to `fetch()` is aborted.
- A URL response with status 299 streams its bytes unchanged.
- A Deno `Response` with status 404 rejects with an error containing the HTTP status.

These regression tests do not cover the new Node `ResponseLike` and web native `Response` paths or the response-backed input reuse checks.

Focused local verification of the final Node async-iterator guard used Node 24.21.0, `node-fetch` 2.7.0, and imported Undici 6.27.0 against a temporary HTTP server on loopback:

- Real `fetch()` responses from all three implementations returned the identical body stream, preserved the exact binary bytes, and made no second request.
- Direct-body 404 responses rejected without consuming their bodies; reusing a successfully selected response-backed `InputFile` rejected.
- Ten null or non-async-iterable body cases, including buffers and non-callable async-iterator properties, followed the URL fallback. A supplied null body with an unsuccessful status also retained the existing fallback behavior.
- A standalone async iterable was returned unchanged, preserved its bytes, and made no second request. Its response-like input retained status rejection and reuse protection.
- Node and WHATWG streams, plus URL fallback, continued to work with the global `ReadableStream` constructor temporarily unavailable. This checks that condition on Node 24; it is not an actual older-Node runtime test.
- `npm run backport`, formatting and lint checks for `src/types.node.ts`, and `git diff --check` passed.

These were focused ad-hoc checks, not additional committed regression tests. They do not establish support for user-constructed responses or byte validation of arbitrary custom streams.

The current PR head is commit `1466e92558501c833e9f017889c84a8058d74337`; its source is available through [pinned jsDelivr imports](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/KnightNiwrem/grammY@1466e92558501c833e9f017889c84a8058d74337/src/mod.ts).

Earlier independent sandbox verification on Deno 2.9.6 exercised commit `5aa566824a4179a493bfb6177d700e4093d7d307`, before the updates to `response.ok` and handling of supplied `Response` bodies:

- HTTP 4xx/5xx failures through URL, `{ url }`, and Deno `Response` inputs rejected with `HttpError.error` containing the original plain status error. Multipart inspection confirmed zero file-body bytes were uploaded.
- Endless 404 URL downloads triggered server-side cancellation after one 1 KiB chunk.
- All 19 live Telegram checks passed: fifteen 404/503 error-source uploads aborted, and four valid HTTP 200 controls succeeded. Three control documents were downloaded and matched byte for byte and by SHA-256; the valid photo was delivered at 64 × 64.
- Sandbox formatting, type checks, and lint passed.

Those sandbox results apply to the earlier commit; the current patch, including Node `ResponseLike` support, web native `Response` support, and reuse checks, has not been rerun in that sandbox. They do not establish cancellation of supplied `Response` bodies under the current patch, which leaves that responsibility to the caller. Runtime verification there covered Deno and the web `InputFile` implementation running in Deno, rather than actual Node or browser runtimes. Valid video/animation controls were not tested.

The fix preserves lazy multipart ordering: the Telegram fetch may start before an unsuccessful source is rejected. The existing `HttpError` wrapper also means auto-retry v2.0.2 retries these failures by default; the earlier sandbox run confirmed that `rethrowHttpErrors: true` propagates them immediately. Retry-policy changes are outside this fix.

title: fix: preserve Bot API 10.3 argument semantics
body:
> [!NOTE]
> This PR was primarily written by GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh in ChatGPT Work.

## Summary

Address two issues found while reviewing #964.

This change:

- preserves `force_reply` when cloning, transposing, reflowing, or copying `Keyboard` and `InlineKeyboard`
- excludes both `text` and `rich_message` from the remaining options for `editEphemeralMessageText`

## Why

Bot API 10.3 adds `force_reply` to reply and inline keyboard markup. The new value was not copied by the keyboard clone paths, so it was lost when a keyboard was cloned, transposed, reflowed, or passed to `from`.

`editEphemeralMessageText` accepts either text or a rich message through its dedicated argument. Its remaining-options type omitted `text`, but not `rich_message`, allowing the options object to override the selected payload or include both fields.

## Verification

- `deno fmt --check` on all changed files
- `npm run backport`
- focused runtime probe against the backported Node output: `force_reply` is preserved across the keyboard copy paths
- focused `deno check` against the current `@grammyjs/types` main branch

The full Deno test entrypoint could not load its remote JSR and Skypack dependencies in the local environment; CI can run the complete suite.
